messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Markus Weber is a 49-year-old city council member who came to treatment after months of telling his wife that he was “fine” and then startling so violently in bed when she reached for his shoulder that she began sleeping more cautiously beside him. He had served in combat years earlier, and when he speaks about the event he still does so in fragments. He remembers being in a convoy and then being on the ground after an explosion, with sound dropping in and out and pieces of the scene coming back without order: dust, shouting, a body too close to him, the sense that he was about to die. What remains most vivid is the terror. When he tries to explain the sequence clearly, he loses the thread, stops mid-sentence, and looks as if he is back there rather than describing it from a distance. The gaps in his memory have taken on meaning for him. Because he can only recall parts of what happened and cannot form a complete account, he has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that his own body cannot be trusted, as if it knows he is under threat before his mind does.

That belief has shaped the way he lives now. Markus is certain that safety is always provisional, something people say to comfort themselves but not something that can be relied on. Even in familiar settings, including council chambers and public meetings he has attended for years, he feels he has to stay on guard. He scans the room automatically, tracks movement in the doorway, and notices who is behind him. When colleagues or constituents reach out to greet him with a hand on the arm or shoulder, he reacts with immediate alarm, his whole body jerking before he can think. The reaction itself frightens him. He has come to see these bodily surges as further proof that his body is working against him, still acting as though the danger is present, and each episode leaves him more convinced that the world really is as unsafe as he feels it to be.

The memories and the threat responses feed each other. At night, when he lies awake unable to settle into sleep, bits of the combat scene intrude more forcefully: the missing pieces remain missing, but the terror arrives intact. On those nights he can feel his body bracing in the dark, listening for sounds in the house, unable to accept his wife’s reassurance that they are safe at home. And after days when he has been especially keyed up—after a crowded council session, or an unexpected touch in a hallway—the memory becomes even less coherent when he tries to think about it, more like shards than a story, with the same original fear rushing back and cutting off his ability to speak.

Over time Markus has developed ways of managing that he experiences as necessary. When images or bodily fear begin to rise, he turns on loud television or music to drown out his own thoughts. He also monitors his mind closely, watching for any sign that he might be “going crazy,” as he puts it, especially when he feels himself losing the thread while remembering. He avoids physical contact whenever he can, sidestepping embraces at public events and keeping a careful distance even from people he likes. In the moment these habits give him something to do, but they also keep him from staying with the memory long enough for it to become clearer. The event remains patchy and unspeakable, and because it remains that way, it continues to return charged with terror rather than as something finished and past.

Those same strategies have deepened his sense that something is wrong with him. The more he orchestrates his day around preventing contact, controlling noise, and checking his own mind for signs of collapse, the more he experiences himself as a man whose body is unpredictable and whose surroundings require constant vigilance. In his work this has become increasingly visible. He now prefers the edge seat in meetings, keeps people out of his personal space during constituent events, and leaves some receptions early because the press of bodies feels intolerable. At home, his wife has experienced him as distant and tense, especially because even ordinary touch can set off an alarmed reaction he cannot hide.

What finally brought him in was not a single flashback or a single bad night, but the recognition that his life had narrowed around staying prepared. He was exhausted from poor sleep, ashamed of recoiling from touch, and increasingly unable to give a straightforward account of the combat event without feeling overwhelmed by the same terror. What frightens him most is the idea that this constant watchfulness means he will never really feel safe again; what he hopes, more quietly, is that he might learn how to be at home in his body and with his wife without bracing for danger.
